Vertex Bootstrap for Network-Level Statistics

Source: R/vertex_bootstrap.R
vertex_bootstrap.Rd

vertex_bootstrap() resamples the nodes of one observed network and returns bootstrap standard errors, bias and confidence intervals for network-level statistics: density, mean weight, strength centralisation and, for a directed network, reciprocity, plus any statistic of your own (Snijders & Borgatti 1999). It needs only the weight matrix, so it works on any netobject or cograph_network, including those that carry no data, such as the constituents of build_mlvar() or the networks as_tna() returns for an mcml object built from a weight matrix, and on a plain square weight matrix.

The intervals describe how much a whole-network statistic depends on which nodes happen to make up the network, with the edge weights taken as given. They say nothing about how the weights themselves vary from sample to sample; when the sequences or rows behind a network are available, bootstrap_network() resamples those instead. Two networks are compared on these statistics with vertex_compare().

Usage

vertex_bootstrap(
  x,
  iter = 1000L,
  ci_level = 0.05,
  ci_method = c("percentile", "basic"),
  statistics = NULL,
  statistic_fn = NULL,
  directed = NULL,
  seed = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'net_vertex_bootstrap'
print(x, digits = 3, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_vertex_bootstrap'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_vertex_bootstrap'
plot(x, bins = 30, ...)

Arguments

x

The network: a netobject (from build_network() or any builder), a cograph_network, or a square numeric weight matrix, with at least 3 nodes. Other input raises an error. For the print() and plot() methods: a net_vertex_bootstrap result.

iter

The number of bootstrap replicates, at least 2. Default 1000.

ci_level

The significance level of the confidence intervals, not their coverage: 0.05 (default) gives 95% intervals. Must lie strictly between 0 and 1.

ci_method

How the intervals are formed. "percentile" (default) takes the ci_level / 2 and 1 - ci_level / 2 quantiles of the replicates; "basic" reflects them around the observed value, 2 * observed - upper and 2 * observed - lower (Davison & Hinkley 1997, eq. 5.6).

statistics

The built-in statistics to compute (see Details). Default NULL: all of them, with reciprocity only for a directed network. A name that is not available for the network, such as reciprocity on an undirected one, raises an error.

statistic_fn

Statistics of your own, as a named list of functions, each taking the weight matrix and returning a single number. They are computed beside the built-ins on the whole matrix, diagonal included. Default NULL.

directed

Whether the network is directed, which decides how collisions are filled and whether reciprocity is available. Default NULL reads the network's own directedness, and for a matrix (or a network that records none) treats an asymmetric matrix as directed.

seed

A seed passed to set.seed() before resampling, so the run can be repeated; the session's random-number stream then continues from it. Default NULL uses the current stream.

digits

For the print() method: the number of decimals shown. Default 3.

...

Not used.

object

For the summary() method: a net_vertex_bootstrap result.

bins

For the plot() method: the number of histogram bins. Default 30.

Value

A net_vertex_bootstrap object. Printing it shows the number of nodes, the directedness, the number of replicates and the interval level and method, then the summary table; summary() returns that table as a data frame with one row per statistic and the columns statistic, observed, boot_mean, boot_sd, bias (boot_mean - observed), ci_lower and ci_upper; plot() draws the bootstrap distributions. The object holds:

summary

The summary table described above.

boot_stats

A matrix of the replicate values, iter rows by one column per statistic.

observed

The observed statistics, as a named numeric vector.

iter, ci_level, ci_method, directed, n_nodes

The settings used and the number of nodes.

The print() method returns its input invisibly, summary() the summary data frame and plot() a ggplot object.

Details

Each replicate draws n node indices with replacement and sets W_b[i, j] = W[idx_i, idx_j]. When the same original node is drawn for two different positions, the off-diagonal cell between them would be a self-pair; following Snijders & Borgatti, it is filled with the weight of a randomly chosen pair of distinct original nodes. Diagonal cells keep the original self-weight of the resampled node (W[idx_i, idx_i]), since self-loops are meaningful in transition networks. For an undirected network the substitution is made in the upper triangle and mirrored, so every replicate stays symmetric.

The built-in statistics are computed on the off-diagonal cells:

density

The share of non-zero off-diagonal cells.

mean_weight

The mean of the non-zero off-diagonal weights.

centralization

Freeman-type strength centralisation, sum(max(s) - s) / ((n - 1) * max(s)), where s is each node's total (in plus out) absolute strength without its self-loop: 0 when every node has the same strength, approaching 1 for a star.

reciprocity

Directed networks only. Weighted reciprocity, sum(pmin(|W|, |t(W)|)) / sum(|W|) over the off-diagonal cells: the share of the total weight that is reciprocated.

A statistic is NA when it is undefined: mean_weight with no non-zero cell, centralization when every strength is 0, reciprocity when the total weight is 0. NA replicates are left out of the bootstrap mean, standard deviation and quantiles.

Methods

plot() draws a histogram of the replicate values for each statistic, one panel per statistic with its own scales, a solid line at the observed value and dashed lines at the interval bounds.

References

Snijders, T. A. B., & Borgatti, S. P. (1999). Non-parametric standard errors and tests for network statistics. Connections, 22(2), 161-170.

Davison, A. C., & Hinkley, D. V. (1997). Bootstrap Methods and their Application. Cambridge University Press.

See also

bootstrap_network for case-resampling edge-weight inference, centrality_stability for case-dropping centrality stability.

Examples

seqs <- data.frame(
  T1 = c("plan", "code", "debug", "plan", "test", "code"),
  T2 = c("code", "debug", "code", "plan", "code", "test"),
  T3 = c("debug", "code", "plan", "code", "debug", "plan"),
  T4 = c("test", "plan", "test", "debug", "plan", "code")
)
net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative")
vb <- vertex_bootstrap(net, iter = 100, seed = 1)
summary(vb)
#>        statistic  observed boot_mean    boot_sd        bias   ci_lower
#> 1        density 0.8333333 0.8433333 0.13415153  0.01000000 0.58333333
#> 2    mean_weight 0.3800000 0.3734656 0.05149123 -0.00653441 0.27899554
#> 3 centralization 0.3589744 0.2255932 0.12632830 -0.13338118 0.04511327
#> 4    reciprocity 0.5939850 0.5726307 0.16772881 -0.02135424 0.13107527
#>    ci_upper
#> 1 1.0000000
#> 2 0.4725536
#> 3 0.4635149
#> 4 0.8545707
# \donttest{
plot(vb)

# }
